title: MINNESOTA WATER SYSTEM CYBERATTACK
executiveAssessment: CONFIRMED FACT HIGH CONFIDENCE Minnesota IT Services (MNIT) publicly stated on July 28, 2026 that a coordinated cyberattack targeted operational technology at more than 30 Minnesota community water systems on July 26 and July 27, 2026. On July 30, 2026, MNIT further stated that most confirmed cases involved technology used to remotely monitor and control equipment, including PLCs and HMIs, and that "impacted" meant investigators confirmed malicious activity involving a system's technology rather than automatic service disruption. Source: MNIT, July 28, 2026 ; MNIT, July 30, 2026 . CONFIRMED FACT HIGH CONFIDENCE Publicly identified affected communities include Braham, Plymouth, South St. Paul, and Maple Plain. Braham and Plymouth published direct municipal statements; South St. Paul and Maple Plain were identified in regional reporting tied to city statements or officials. Source: City of Plymouth, July 27, 2026 ; AP, July 30, 2026 ; Star Tribune, July 28, 2026 ; MPR News, July 27, 2026 . CONFIRMED FACT HIGH CONFIDENCE Public evidence supports that some systems were forced into manual operation or contingency procedures, but available public evidence does not support claims of confirmed drinking-water contamination or confirmed public-health harm in Minnesota. State and local statements consistently said water quality remained unaffected in the publicly identified communities. Source: MNIT, July 30, 2026 ; City of Plymouth ; AP . ASSESSMENT MODERATE CONFIDENCE The incidents appear operationally related at least at a campaign level because of common timing, common sector targeting, and common affected technology classes, all of which were acknowledged by MNIT. However, available public evidence is insufficient to conclude that every incident in Minnesota was executed by the same actor or through the same access path. MNIT explicitly stated that similarities existed but investigators had not determined that every incident was carried out by the same actor. Source: MNIT, July 30, 2026 . UNRESOLVED MODERATE CONFIDENCE Public attribution remains unresolved. Minnesota expressly stated that it had not attributed the activity to a specific actor. Some national reporting said U.S. officials were investigating possible Iranian involvement across multiple states, but those same reports said attribution was not definitive and could change. That does not meet the threshold for confirmed attribution. Source: MNIT, July 30, 2026 ; CBS News, updated Aug. 1, 2026 . Bottom line: the public record establishes a real, multi-community, OT-focused cyber event affecting more than 30 Minnesota community water systems on July 26-27, 2026. It establishes temporary operational disruption and manual fallback in some communities. It does not publicly establish the specific initial-access vector, any released IOC set, any named malware family used in Minnesota, or a confirmed threat actor.

keyFindings.title: Statewide OT Targeting

keyFindings.title: Primary Affected Technology Types
keyFindings.text: Most confirmed cases involved remote monitoring and control technology, including PLCs and HMIs. Supporting evidence: MNIT, July 30, 2026.

keyFindings.title: Operational Disruption, Not Proven Water Contamination
keyFindings.text: Some communities used manual operations or contingency procedures; public evidence does not show confirmed water-quality compromise in Minnesota. Supporting evidence: MNIT; City of Plymouth; AP on Braham.

keyFindings.title: Common Campaign Characteristics
keyFindings.text: Timing and technology similarities support a shared-campaign hypothesis, but not full common-authorship confirmation. Supporting evidence: MNIT explicitly cited similarities while withholding a same-actor conclusion.

keyFindings.title: Initial Access Details Withheld
keyFindings.text: MNIT said it identified methods of access but would not release access details or system-specific forensic findings during the active investigation. Supporting evidence: MNIT, July 30, 2026.

keyFindings.title: Attribution Not Established Publicly
keyFindings.text: Possible Iran-related reporting exists, but no authoritative public attribution for the Minnesota incidents alone was established in the reviewed record. Supporting evidence: MNIT; CBS News reporting; AP fact-check.

timeline: Date / Time Event Source Classification Confidence Overnight July 26, 2026 Plymouth reported outage began overnight Sunday, July 26, affecting communications at two water towers and multiple lift stations; cause suspected to be a cyberattack. City of Plymouth CONFIRMED FACT HIGH July 26-27, 2026 MNIT said a coordinated cyberattack targeted operational technology at more than 30 Minnesota community water systems. MNIT, July 28 CONFIRMED FACT HIGH July 27, 2026 (morning) Braham asked residents to minimize water use for several hours while the water plant was offline; later described as due to a cyberattack. AP ; MPR News CONFIRMED FACT HIGH July 27, 2026 ~90 minutes National reporting said Braham isolated the affected system, restored a backup, and restarted the plant in about 90 minutes; residents relied on water held in the tower while plant controls were affected. CBS News ; AP CONFIRMED FACT MODERATE July 27, 2026 2:05 p.m. Plymouth announced communications had been restored and stated water levels and quality were unaffected throughout the outage. City of Plymouth CONFIRMED FACT HIGH July 28, 2026 MNIT publicly activated and announced statewide cyber response with state, federal, local, Tribal, and private-sector partners. MNIT, July 28 CONFIRMED FACT HIGH July 28, 2026 Star Tribune reported South St. Paul switched to manual operations and Maple Plain declared a local state of emergency and implemented contingency procedures for water and wastewater operations. Star Tribune ASSESSMENT MODERATE July 30, 2026 MNIT said most confirmed cases involved PLCs and HMIs, there were no active requests to modify drinking-water use, and Minnesota had not attributed activity to a specific actor. MNIT, July 30 CONFIRMED FACT HIGH Aug. 1, 2026 CBS reported federal investigators were probing possible Iranian involvement in similar water-system activity in at least seven states, but attribution was not definitive. CBS News INVESTIGATIVE LEAD LOW
methodology: Confirmed Activity CONFIRMED FACT Activity targeted operational technology at more than 30 community water systems on July 26-27, 2026. Source: MNIT . CONFIRMED FACT Most confirmed cases involved technology used for remote monitoring and control , including PLCs and HMIs. Source: MNIT . CONFIRMED FACT In Braham, attackers reportedly shut down operating controls that shut down the well and water treatment plant. Source: AP . CONFIRMED FACT In Plymouth, the event affected communications between water infrastructure components, and manual procedures sustained operations. Source: City of Plymouth . CONFIRMED FACT MNIT publicly said it had identified methods of access but did not disclose them. Source: MNIT . Assessed Activity ASSESSMENT MODERATE CONFIDENCE The activity likely involved unauthorized access to remote-management or remote-monitoring pathways for OT, because MNIT emphasized remote monitoring/control technology and the local effects centered on communications, controls, and remote operation. This remains an assessment, not a confirmed public forensic finding. UNRESOLVED Initial access mechanism: UNRESOLVED . UNRESOLVED Credential compromise vs. vulnerability exploitation vs. default/weak credentials: UNRESOLVED . UNRESOLVED Use of malware, custom ladder logic, defacement, persistence mechanisms, or C2: NOT PUBLICLY VERIFIED . UNRESOLVED IT-to-OT movement: NOT PUBLICLY VERIFIED . Relevant Comparison Context, Not Proof of Method in Minnesota CISA and partner advisories before 2026 documented multiple water-sector and OT compromises involving internet-exposed PLC/HMI environments, default passwords, and weak remote access, including the Unitronics advisory on IRGC-affiliated actors and the broader OT fact sheet on pro-Russia hacktivist activity. Those materials are relevant for defensive context but do not prove that the Minnesota incidents used the same products, same vulnerabilities, or same actor. correlation: Supported Similarities Same time window: July 26-27, 2026. Source: MNIT . Same sector: community water systems. Source: MNIT . Same technology class: remote monitoring/control OT, PLCs, HMIs. Source: MNIT . Similar local effects: communications loss, automated control disruption, fallback to manual procedures. Sources: Plymouth ; AP ; Star Tribune . Key Limits on Correlation MNIT specifically said investigators had not determined that every incident was carried out by the same actor. Source: MNIT . ASSESSMENT MODERATE CONFIDENCE The Minnesota incidents are best described as potentially related coordinated activity or a shared campaign of similar OT targeting , rather than a conclusively single intrusion set. CONFIRMED FACT MODERATE CONFIDENCE National reporting said similar malicious activity affected water systems in at least seven states in late July 2026, including Minnesota and Michigan, and referenced Clayton County, Georgia as another case under investigation. Sources: CBS News ; AP, Aug. 1, 2026 ; Clayton County Water Authority, Aug. 3, 2026 . External Incident Observed Similarity Relationship Assessment Basis Michigan water systems, late July / early Aug. 2026 Same general period; water-sector targeting; issues addressed by local operators; no known public-health impact reported. POSSIBLE RELATIONSHIP CBS and AP reported federal investigators were treating the activity as multi-state, but no public technical linkage was released. Clayton County Water Authority, Georgia, July 27, 2026 Same date; utility investigated unauthorized cyber activity; temporary operational disruption; public-health protocol boil advisory triggered by reduced pressure and later lifted. POSSIBLE RELATIONSHIP CCWA statement ; CBS referenced it in multi-state context. 2023-2024 Unitronics / CyberAv3ngers-related water incidents Water-sector OT targeting; PLC/HMI focus; concern around exposed ICS and weak/default credentials. SIMILAR ACTIVITY Relevant historical analogy only; no public evidence proves same product, same exploit path, or same actor in Minnesota. ASSESSMENT LOW CONFIDENCE There is enough public reporting to say the Minnesota incidents occurred amid a broader late-July 2026 pattern of water-system cyber activity in multiple states. There is not enough public evidence to merge all such incidents into one confirmed campaign with one confirmed operator.

sections.heading: AFFECTED SYSTEMS
sections.text: Confirmed or Publicly Identified Organizations / Communities More than 30 Minnesota community water systems - confirmed by MNIT. Source: MNIT . Plymouth - city stated communications issue affected two water towers and multiple lift stations; manual procedures used; no water-quality impact. Source: City of Plymouth . Braham - plant outage, well and treatment plant controls affected, temporary reliance on tower water, no water-quality issue reported. Source: AP ; MPR News . South St. Paul - manual operations reported while automated controls restored. Source: Star Tribune . Maple Plain - local emergency declaration and contingency procedures for water and wastewater operations reported. Source: Star Tribune . Confirmed Technology / OT Components Operational technology used to remotely monitor and control equipment. Source: MNIT . PLCs. Source: MNIT . HMIs. Source: MNIT . Communications-connected infrastructure including towers and lift stations in Plymouth. Source: City of Plymouth . Not Publicly Verified Specific PLC or HMI vendor used in the Minnesota incidents. Specific SCADA software or engineering workstation product involved. Whether the affected environments were internet-exposed. Whether VPN, cellular modem, VNC, RDP, web interface, or vendor remote management was used for access. Whether any wastewater-only systems, rather than drinking-water systems, were directly compromised in the same event set. Any IOC set, hash, domain, IP, or forensic artifact released by authorities for these incidents. MNIT stated it had identified methods of access but would not release system-specific forensic findings, network indicators, or access details while the investigation remained active. Source: MNIT, July 30, 2026 .

sections.heading: INTELLIGENCE GAPS
sections.text: Exact list of all affected Minnesota communities and systems. Initial access vector(s) for each confirmed incident. Whether access relied on internet-exposed OT, VPN, remote desktop, cellular links, vendor remote support, or compromised credentials. Specific PLC/HMI/SCADA products and versions involved. sections.heading: INVESTIGATIVE LEADS
sections.text: Obtain local emergency declarations, council minutes, or after-action records from Maple Plain, South St. Paul, Braham, and other municipalities for system-specific impact detail. Monitor MNIT, CISA, FBI, EPA, and Minnesota Department of Health for any delayed release of advisories, anonymized findings, or sector notices. Seek public-record releases on incident response procurement, temporary control-system services, and recovery expenditures by affected communities. Compare late-July 2026 incidents in Michigan and Georgia for any subsequently disclosed common product or access-path indicators. Review whether any later federal advisory references July 2026 multi-state water incidents with technical detail. Check whether water operators or local governments later published 2026 annual reports, board packets, or budget amendments containing cyber incident recovery details.

sections.heading: FINAL ASSESSMENT
sections.text: WHAT DO WE KNOW? A real cyber event affected more than 30 Minnesota community water systems on July 26-27, 2026. The activity targeted OT used for remote monitoring and control, including PLCs and HMIs. At least some communities experienced loss of automated control/communications and shifted to manual or contingency operations. Publicly named communities include Braham, Plymouth, South St. Paul, and Maple Plain. Available public evidence does not show confirmed drinking-water contamination or confirmed public-health harm in Minnesota from these incidents. Minnesota had not publicly attributed the activity to a specific actor in the reviewed record. WHAT DO WE ASSESS? The activity was likely a coordinated campaign or overlapping set of coordinated intrusions against similar water-sector OT environments. The attackers likely leveraged remote-access or remote-management exposure associated with OT operations, but the public record does not establish the exact access path. The incidents demonstrate a real operational risk to smaller and mid-sized water utilities even where water quality remains protected through manual fallback and operator intervention. WHAT DO WE SUSPECT? There may have been a broader multi-state wave of similar activity during late July 2026. Credential weakness, exposed remote services, or insecure OT connectivity are plausible enabling conditions, but this remains hypothesis-level absent public forensic proof for Minnesota. Possible Iran-linked involvement was under federal scrutiny in media reporting, but that remains unconfirmed for this case set. WHAT DON'T WE KNOW? The specific initial-access mechanism(s). The exact list of all affected utilities. The products, versions, and configurations compromised. Whether a single actor or multiple actors were responsible. Whether any common infrastructure, malware, or credential set linked the victims. The full cost and operational burden of recovery across the state. WHAT EVIDENCE WOULD CHANGE THE ASSESSMENT? A state or federal technical advisory with IOCs, victimology, or access-path details. Municipal after-action reports identifying compromised technology and method of access. Vendor or forensic findings tying systems together through shared artifacts. Official attribution by government backed by technical and intelligence evidence. Public records showing confirmed equipment damage, water-quality effects, or broader service interruption. Final analytic judgment: the strongest defensible conclusion is that Minnesota experienced a coordinated, OT-focused cyber event against community water systems during July 26-27, 2026, with real but mostly contained operational consequences and no publicly verified water-quality harm. The exact intrusion method and attribution remain unresolved. Primary sources reviewed included Minnesota IT Services, Minnesota Department of Health guidance, City of Plymouth, Clayton County Water Authority, and major regional/national reporting used primarily for corroboration and lead development. Significant source dependencies were considered; repeated media restatements of MNIT were not treated as independent corroboration of underlying forensic facts.
